sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Urartu
sources.note: Direct institutional overview, fortresses and provincial administration, Tushpa, Ayanis outer town. Its older blanket destruction chronology and erroneous late-ninth-century Karmir Blur statement are not adopted.

sources.title: Wolfram Kleiss: Urartu in Iran, Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.note: Direct scholarly historical outline: mid-ninth-century political unity, eastern expansion, governors, continued kingdom after 714 BCE. Page accidentally calls campaign king Sargon I; use independently established Sargon II, with Met essay corroboration, or omit personal name. No automatic single Median conquest adopted.

sources.title: Armenia’s 2025 heritage submission: Erebuni and Karmir Blur
sources.note: State-party Tentative List submission, not UNESCO endorsement or World Heritage inscription. Checked Description and Archaeological Setting sections: royal 6600 captive claim, Erebuni frescoes and pebble street, continued occupation. Avoid speculative script ancestry, confident conqueror assignments, and conflating Xenophon with Urartian period.

sources.title: Visit Yerevan: Ancient city of Teishebaini (Karmir Blur)
sources.note: Municipal visitor platform, residential district paragraph: seventh/sixth-century houses, 6m street, large plus 5 to 6 small rooms, wood/reed roofs, hearths and grain pits. Page has other chronology/royal genealogy errors not adopted.

sources.title: Solmaz and Oybak Dönmez: Archaeobotanical studies at Ayanis
sources.note: Original 2013 Turkish Journal of Botany 37(2),282 to 296, DOI10.3906/bot-1204-3. Full indexed original abstract checked; direct page omits abstract. Charred grain, SEM suggests bulgur-like food, caraway/coriander/parsley fruits; medicinal interpretation based on folkloric analogy, explicitly uncertain.

sources.title: Yerevan Municipality: Urartian caravanserai unearthed at Karmir Blur
sources.note: 8 December 2021 original municipal report; full indexed text directly quotes Erebuni Museum director Mikael Badalyan. Royal stable interpreted, possible caravanserai; paved floor, massive walls, round-column bases and timber roof. Earlier shortened URL was incorrect; this is successful original URL.

sources.title: eCUT A 05-012: Minua canal rock inscription
sources.note: ORACC primary scholarly edition CTU A05-012, ninth/eighth century, Kadembas, Minua son of Ishpuini. Indexed original full transliteration and English checked. Line3 mì-nu-a-i pi-li ti-i-ni; person determinative m omitted in public simplified scholarly transcription, no cuneiform glyph reconstruction. Lines1 to 3 translation and lines7 to 14 curse checked.

sources.title: eCUT A 12-02: Rusa’s Karmir Blur temple inscription
sources.note: Original full indexed scholarly edition CTU A12-02, seventh-century temple block. Obverse column i1 to 7, ii1: susi temple, Rusa son of Argishti, Haldi, named animal sacrifices. Public text avoids damaged and untranslated portions and does not turn barren-land royal rhetoric into settlement archaeology.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Part of a throne with deity on a bull
sources.note: Direct object50.163, late eighth/seventh century, bronze with plastic restoration, probably Toprakkale. Curator says most likely throne part; reconstruction based on better preserved examples, not intact surviving throne.

sources.title: Emily Hammer: Role and Characteristics of Irrigation in the Kingdom of Urartu
sources.note: 2022 OIS13 chapter10, begins printed269; exact checked passage printed270, Urartu: Inscriptions, Fortresses, Environment, first paragraph and notes4 to 6. Direct PDF errors; indexed original excerpts explicitly report debated destruction dates/attackers and proposed mid-seventh through early/mid-sixth-century dates. Publisher contents confirms author/chapter. No precise terminal year or definitive invader asserted. Irrigation discussion distinguishes local from royal action.
